Q: How can I boxplot values that wrap around using matplotlib? A:

Preprocessing your data is probably your best bet. I just used the unwrap function from numpy, which yielded some decent results:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Generate dummy data
alpha = [-150, -120, -90, 90, 120, 150, 180]
PDOA_true = [
    rng.normal(mean, std, size=(15))
    for mean, std
    in [(-119, 4), (125, 8), (150, 4), (-145, 35), (145, 5), (-179, 3), (150, 10)]
]
PDOA_wrapped = [
    (arr + 180) % 360 - 180
    for arr in PDOA_true
]

# Preprocessing data: unwrapping
PDOA_unwrapped = [
    np.unwrap(arr, period=360)
    for arr in PDOA_wrapped
]

# Display boxplot
plt.close('all')

plt.boxplot(PDOA_unwrapped, orientation='vertical', positions=alpha, widths = 10)

plt.plot([-180, 180], [-180, 180], color='grey', linewidth=1, alpha=0.3)

plt.grid()
ticks = list(range(-180, 181, 30))
plt.xticks(ticks, [str(t) for t in ticks])
plt.xlim([-180, 180])
# plt.ylim([-180, 180]) # /!\ No ylim since the boxplot might extend outside of them


plt.show()

Please note that unwrapping is not necessarily easy, and unwrap can have issues with some configurations.

Q: How to use a different AI agent (not GitHub Copilot) in Visual Studio's Agent Mode? A:

No. The Agent Mode is a GitHub Copilot feature and uses GitHub Copilot to orchestrate the task.

For Visual Studio Code there are extensions from other providers, like Codex, that can handle your work, but they don't integrate into the GitHub Copilot UI, they bring their own chat panel.

In other IDE's like Jetbrains' Rider, there is common chat panel with multiple providers. But for Visual Studio (Code) this is currently not extensible for other providers.

Now there are a few people who built CLI wrappers or proxy servers that actually intercept the message from the Chat panel and route it differently. But these are often a bit hacky, from untrusted publishers and may break at any time. It might work for you, but your mileage may vary.

BTW: Visual Studio 2026 brought a much more extensive version of Copilot, so you may want to upgrade.

Q: What happens in an interrupt service routine? A:

When we look in terms of the software interrupt, like needing hardware, then these interrupts will come into the picture. Suppose if we want to print the value on the screen (written in a C program). Here writing on Monitor means we need operating system support. We can't write directly. If that is the case, anyone can write anything. The CPU will stop its execution and that interrupt will be serviced first. It will leads to call the system call.

A system call is a special type of function which is going to be in the OS code. When ever you are writing normal function in the C program the caller and callee both are in the same program, i.e., at the same address. But when you are calling the OS code's function, we need a system call which acts as an entry point to the kernel code. This function can't be accessed by the user without the system call.

The compiler will converts the given C code to assembly code. So whenever you write the "printf("hello")", in the assembly code it will be 'rax 50,syscall', where rax is a register. Once the 'syscall' instruction is seen by the CPU, it'll go to the rax register and find the appropriate number for that syscall as there more than 400 system calls in the OS. Now the CPU will go to the system call table (interrupt vector table) and find the address of that 50.

Address of that 50 is function pointer which is 'sys_write'. It also takes arguments like "hello", in order to print on the screen and CPU will execute the code of the function sys_write in the kernel mode (OS) which is to be the interrupt service routine. Once that interrupt service routine is done with the help of a function pointer, then CPU will get back to the user mode.

For the fun(), fun is pointer to that function.
